Capital One. What's in your wallet?
Terms apply. Details at CapitalOne.com.
The thing that's more relevant is what is the generic congressional ballot in just those dozen or so competitive seats.
And there are some polls that measure that.
And those polls show that instead of 8 or 9 or 11 points ahead, as Democrats are nationally in the generic ballot question,
in those competitive seats there are only 2 or 3 points ahead.
So it tells you how close those competitive House races are.
And those are the races that are going to determine how big a majority Democrats get if they win the House.
That's NPR's Marl Eiasson. Alaska's Democratic Senate candidate is rescheduling her campaign events after a car crash.
And Pierre's Chantalice Duster has our details.
Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign says the Democrat and her family were struck by a driver while on their way to a campaign event Saturday night.
Cheryl Bruce, Peltola's campaign manager, said in a statement they sustained "minor injuries but are in good spirits."
She also said Peltola is disappointed by the delay the accident has caused and is eager to get back on the campaign trail.
Her campaign says events will be rescheduled in the coming days.
Peltola was set to visit eight communities over the next seven days up to the midterm elections as part of an Alaska Always Tour.
The former Congresswoman is challenging Republican Senator Dan Sullivan.
She made history in 2022 as the first Alaska native sworn into Congress.
Chantalice Duster, NPR News.
A student-led list of parliamentary candidates that began as a protest movement against corruption has defeated the party of longtime Serbian leader Alexander Vucic.
As NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports, the victory of the student list has created a political earthquake in the small but influential Balkan country.
Serbia's capital of Belgrade erupted in joy and pandemonium Sunday after President Alexander Vucic conceded that his Serbian Progressive Party had lost to what is simply known as "the student list."
Vucic, who served as information minister for Serb Strongman Slobodan Milosevic in the late '90s, has been president of Serbia for 14 years.
It's crazy out here. Everyone's screaming victory, victory. It's everyone celebrating that we got rid of corruption and primitivism.
22-year-old law student Petar Wojnowicz is part of the protest movement that began two years ago and attracted voters well beyond university campuses by becoming a powerful expression of dissatisfaction with corruption and a lack of accountability.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News.
Shares in Asia are falling after a retreat last week on Wall Street, but U.S. futures are up slightly. Oil prices have fallen more than one percent.
This is NPR News.
For the first time since December, Nobel laureate Maria Corina Machado is back in Venezuela. She announced her return in a social media post.
The opposition leader is returning from exile at a time when doubts are growing about the country's democratic future.
It was her first appearance in the country since the U.S. military deposed the country's then-president, Nicolas Maduro, in January.
Researchers are now documenting the deadly toll of this summer's extreme heat in Western Europe.
Ampere Zeva Burger reports on new findings about the loss of life.
50,000. That's how many people researchers estimate died in Europe this summer due to the sweltering heat.
It marked the highest number of heat-related deaths ever recorded for the region.
Researchers say climate change made that number so high.
Two new papers from London looked at hundreds of urban areas across Europe.
They found that temperatures on the continent this summer were 4.5 degrees Fahrenheit hotter than they would have been without climate change.
That may not sound like much, but they found that additional heat likely drove 60 percent of those heat-related deaths.
The majority of the deaths were among the elderly.
Ampere Zeva Burger, NPR News.
DC Studios scored a modest, star-rated hit in movie theater this weekend.
Clay Face had a $24 million opening weekend big enough to land in first place.
The documentary "You Can See Everything" continued its strong showing, bringing in $19.5 million in ticket sales from North American theaters.
And the stop-motion animation flick "Wildwood" ended in third, bringing in $11.8 million in ticket sales.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.
